Daniel’s list is most revealing not as a canon of “best games,” but as a consistent aesthetic: games that treat *structure itself* as the artwork—spatially (Antichamber’s topology), temporally (Outer Wilds’ loop as level design), narratively (Stanley Parable’s branching as the point), or systemically (Cataclysm DDA’s simulation as plot engine). That’s close to a formalist tradition in game criticism: the sense that meaning is produced by rules, constraints, and layout as much as by “story,” and it echoes the proceduralist view that games persuade and move us through their systems (see [Ian Bogost, *Persuasive Games*](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262529858/persuasive-games/)). If Daniel wants the term “structural beauty” to do real work (rather than remain a tasteful gesture toward GEB), it would help to discriminate *kinds* of structure: authored puzzle-logic (Portal 2), self-contradicting space (Antichamber), recursive narration (Stanley Parable), and emergent simulation (Cataclysm) are not the same pleasure, and they sometimes pull against “vibe” and pacing rather than supporting them.

The most interesting hidden assumption is in the praise for “metagame” and “suspension of disbelief,” especially around OneShot: Daniel treats immersion as the goal, even when the device is fourth-wall rupture. That’s a coherent stance, but it’s also a choice. A large lineage of modern art uses *anti-immersion*—foregrounding the frame—to create clarity rather than belief (Brecht is the classic reference point), and many “metagames” oscillate between intimacy and distance rather than simply deepening immersion. Naming that tension would sharpen the criteria: is the highest compliment that a game makes Daniel “believe,” or that it makes Daniel notice the machinery—and if both, *how* does it alternate those modes without collapsing into gimmick?

Finally, the post’s biggest omission isn’t a missing title but a missing axis: “notable” seems to mean “innovative and personally affecting,” yet those are different standards. The list is heavy on authored experiences (puzzles, narrative design, vibes) and relatively light on competitive strategy, long-horizon mastery, or community-driven forms where structure emerges socially (beyond Keep Talking / SCP:SL). That’s not a flaw in taste, but it matters for the argument’s implied scope: without acknowledging those other game-structures—rank ladders, mod ecologies, metagame economies—the essay risks quietly equating “structural beauty” with the kinds of structures that resemble literature and architecture, and overlooking the ones that resemble institutions.
